planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry tolerates wet, poorly drained sites and standing water better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen shrub, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and low, boggy spots. Plant both a male and a female cultivar nearby if berries are wanted, since the species is dioecious.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is exceptionally tolerant of wet feet and periodic flooding, unusual among broadleaf evergreens, and also handles drier upland soils once established. Ilex glabra is a native evergreen holly of the wet pinelands, pocosins, and coastal plain wetlands of the eastern and Gulf Coast United States, valued in the landscape as a fine-textured, small-leaved, boxwood-like substitute that thrives in acidic, poorly drained soils where boxwood struggles. Small, inconspicuous white flowers in late spring give way, on female plants, to small black berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for songbirds. The dense, upright to rounded habit takes shearing well, making it a popular choice for a low hedge, foundation planting, or naturalistic screen in a partly shaded woodland-edge landscape. A tough, adaptable, wildlife-valuable native evergreen for difficult wet or acidic sites, zone 4–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; sweetleaf is a true understory species of southeastern woodlands and performs best sited beneath a high pine or hardwood canopy rather than in open sun.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees; adaptable to a range of soil textures as long as it is not waterlogged. Symplocos tinctoria (sweetleaf, or horse sugar) is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub or small tree of southeastern woodlands, named for its distinctly sweet-tasting leaves — historically browsed eagerly by livestock (hence 'horse sugar') and once used by farmers as emergency fodder. In late winter to earliest spring, before or as new leaves emerge, the bare branches are lined with small, fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters that provide an important early nectar source for native bees at a time when little else is blooming. The foliage is a larval host plant for several moth species, including the striking io moth, adding real ecological value to a woodland garden planting. An underused, ecologically valuable native for the shaded understory of a southeastern woodland garden, zone 6–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Ruby Spice tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils and is an excellent choice for a rain garden or pond-edge planting in dappled shade.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, though it tolerates more sun with consistently wet soil; keep evenly moist, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought. Ruby Spice is a pink-flowered cultivar of the native summersweet, Clethra alnifolia, bred to hold a deeper, more saturated rose-pink flower color through its whole bloom period than older pink selections, which often fade toward white as the flowers age. In mid-to-late summer, dense, upright, bottlebrush-like flower spikes release an intensely sweet, spicy fragrance that carries well through the garden and draws heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. The glossy, dark green foliage turns clear yellow in fall before drop. An outstanding fragrant, pollinator-rich choice for a partly shaded, consistently moist border or woodland-edge planting, zone 4–9.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Walter's viburnum tolerates both wet, low sites and drier upland soils once established, and takes shearing well when grown as a formal hedge.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; adaptable to both periodically wet and average garden soils, and tolerates shearing into a formal hedge as well as being left to grow into a graceful large natural shrub or small tree. Viburnum obovatum (Walter's viburnum) is a native evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub of wetland margins, stream banks, and hammocks across the Gulf South and Florida, distinguished from other native viburnums by its small, glossy, finely textured leaves that give it a refined, boxwood-like appearance even without pruning. In late winter to early spring, the branches are covered in small, fragrant, white flower clusters that draw abundant pollinators, followed by small red fruits that ripen to black and are readily eaten by songbirds. Its fine texture, evergreen habit, and tolerance of both hedge shearing and natural form make it one of the most versatile native shrubs for a Gulf South screen, hedge, or woodland-edge planting, zone 7–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Little Honey's golden foliage colors best with some morning sun but scorches in hot, direct afternoon sun, especially in the Gulf South — site with afternoon shade protection.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; keep evenly watered, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry, hot conditions. Little Honey is a compact, dwarf, golden-leaved sport of the classic native oakleaf hydrangea, Hydrangea quercifolia, selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-gold in spring and holds strong golden color through summer before turning shades of orange-red in fall — a dramatic color echo of the oakleaf's already excellent native fall display. Creamy white, cone-shaped flower panicles appear in early summer, aging to soft pink, though the golden foliage is the primary draw of this compact cultivar, which stays considerably smaller than the species and fits well into smaller shaded gardens where a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea would be too large. An outstanding foliage-color accent for a partly shaded border, zone 5–9.
